# Introduction

**Electroencephalography (EEG)** is widely utilized for its unparalleled temporal resolution, which allows researchers to study neural dynamics _in vivo_. However, as measurements are primarily recorded at the scalp, the technique suffers from poor spatial resolution. In 1993, the **Minimum Norm Estimate (MNE)** was introduced to project EEG data onto a cortical surface modeled from individual MRI [@dale_improved_1993]. This approach, broadly termed **source reconstruction**, aimed to combine the high temporal resolution of EEG with the spatial precision of structural imaging.

Despite three decades of evolution into a diverse array of variants (e.g., sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], LCMV [@van_veen_localization_1997]), these methods are still primarily used to identify isolated brain regions — a practice often called **source localization** [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. This focus on localization overlooks a fundamental shift in modern neuroscience toward **connectomics**. As the "localizationist" view reaches its theoretical limits, it is being superseded by **connectivity neuroscience**, which treats the brain as an integrated system of interacting networks rather than a collection of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010].

Widely used source reconstruction methods — such as sLORETA, eLORETA, dSPM, and LCMV — remain largely ill-suited for this shift because they rely on the assumption of **independent sources**, a prior known to perform worse than one informed by the true source covariance structure [@wipf_unified_2009]. This assumption is defensible when activity is genuinely focal — for example, identifying the cortical onset of a sensory stimulus or an epileptic spike — but breaks down as soon as multiple brain regions are simultaneously involved. Because the EEG inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed due to volume conduction, reconstructed activity from interacting sources blurs together across the cortex, a phenomenon known as **leakage** [@schoffelen_source_2009]. A structured prior on source interactions cannot remove this ill-posedness, but, unlike the independent-sources assumption, it can mitigate leakage's impact [@gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies have been proposed to address this. Some methods incorporate functional priors from fMRI to constrain expected source interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021]; however, this approach is constrained by the mismatch between fMRI's hemodynamic response, which unfolds over seconds, and the millisecond-scale dynamics of EEG source activity, limiting how precisely such a prior can constrain the interactions it is meant to inform. Others take an agnostic approach, jointly estimating source activities and their unknown covariance structure from the data itself — a family exemplified by **BC-VARETA** [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018], at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computational expense. A third strategy draws on the growing body of evidence for **structure–function coupling**: since neural activity is known to propagate along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography provides a principled and subject-specific prior for source reconstruction [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

**Graph Signal Processing (GSP)** provides the mathematical machinery to exploit this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. By applying eigendecomposition to the connectome's graph Laplacian, one obtains an orthonormal set of **brain harmonics** — eigenvectors ordered by their associated graph frequency [@atasoy_human_2016]. Low-frequency harmonics capture smooth, globally integrated patterns of activity; high-frequency harmonics encode more locally segregated ones. Projecting source activity onto this eigenbasis — the **Graph Fourier Transform (GFT)** — yields a compact representation termed the **connectome spectrum**. Crucially, recent work has demonstrated that both fMRI and EEG source activity are highly compact in this domain: activity energy concentrates predominantly in low-frequency harmonics and decays following an inverse curve, reflecting the tendency of brain dynamics to align with the smooth, integrative modes of the structural connectome [@atasoy_human_2016; @rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. **Rué-Queralt et al. (2024)** leveraged this principle to introduce **Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET)**: a source reconstruction method that enforces an L₁ sparsity prior directly in the connectome spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics and thereby embedding structural organisation into the reconstruction.

Similar concepts have been explored using the **Beltrami-Laplace operator** applied to the cortical mesh rather than the connectome's graph Laplacian [@pang_geometric_2023]. This substitutes white matter tractography with the local geometry of the gray matter surface, capturing fine-grained short-range connectivity at the expense of the long-range structural pathways defined by white matter tracts. **Pang et al. (2023)** showed that geometric eigenmodes derived this way reconstruct functional brain activity at least as accurately as eigenmodes derived from structural connectomes, indicating that cortical geometry alone can yield spectral representations of neural signals that are comparably compact to connectome-based ones [@pang_geometric_2023]. Building on this, **Wang et al. (2026)** developed **Geometric Basis Functions (GBF)**, representing whole-brain EEG/MEG activity as a linear combination of the leading ~200 Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical surface (capturing ~87% of cortical variance), regularized by an L₂ penalty whose weight decays exponentially across eigenvalue-ordered geometric modes [@wang_geometry_2026]. **Pok Him Siu et al.**, by contrast, proposed a weighted spectral method based on SVD truncation of the forward operator: the weighted Beltrami-operator harmonics act as a hard spectral filter applied after source reconstruction — determining which components are retained — rather than as a continuous penalty embedded in the optimization itself [@siu_structural_2026].

So far, CSET has no principled way to distinguish biologically meaningful harmonics from those dominated by noise, unlike the geometry-based methods described above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction. In this work, we address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces the L₁ prior with a weighted L₂ prior whose penalties follow an exponential decay on graph frequency — resembling GBF's continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian rather than the cortical mesh's Beltrami-Laplace operator. Such a weighting is well justified by the findings of **Abdelnour et al. (2018)** [@abdelnour_functional_2018], who show that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural connectome Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so that a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes dominate functional connectivity — consistent with the broader tendency of brain signal energy to concentrate in, and decay across, low graph frequencies [@huang_graph_2016]. Unlike the geometry-based approaches described above, the graph used here is a connectome that is fully aware of the underlying white matter tracts.

Despite this progression from a fixed L₁ sparsity prior to increasingly principled, geometry- and connectome-informed spectral weightings, a critical gap remains in how these methods have actually been validated. **Rué-Queralt et al.** validated CSET by correlating reconstructed source activity with fMRI data from the same task. Yet fMRI measures hemodynamic responses — blood oxygenation changes driven by neurovascular coupling — which reflect neural activity only indirectly and with significant temporal blurring. The resulting mismatch between EEG source reconstructions and fMRI extends well beyond what correlation can account for, and constitutes a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. The remaining works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients. While some report improvements in estimated source extent, this evaluation criterion is fundamentally misaligned with the ambition of connectivity-informed methods: their value lies not in refining the spatial footprint of a focal source, but in capturing the dynamic propagation of activity across interconnected networks — a capability that localization accuracy simply cannot measure.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is therefore the lack of a **ground truth for interconnected neural dynamics**. We address this gap by reviving and extending the framework proposed by **Grova et al. (2016)** [@grova_intracranial_2016], who correlated MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from the same patients. Here, we extend this framework to truly simultaneous EEG and iEEG recordings. Unlike fMRI or localization benchmarks, iEEG directly measures electrical potential within the brain — free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring — making it the only available electrophysiological ground truth for dynamic source reconstruction. By projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations, we obtain two directly comparable datasets — **estimated iEEG** and **true iEEG** — providing an electrophysiologically grounded benchmark for evaluating source reconstruction beyond localization.

We utilize this framework alongside a clinical localization cohort to evaluate **CSET** and **wCSET** across three complementary studies:

- **Study I:** Using simulations of spontaneous source diffusion via dMRI-based structural connectivity, we demonstrate that while standard methods accurately localize a source's _onset_, connectivity-informed methods are significantly superior at capturing its _propagation_. We also assess the robustness of these methods against dataerroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** Using a clinical epilepsy dataset where post-surgical success defines the ground truth, we show that connectivity-informed methods preserve localization accuracy comparable to gold-standard clinical algorithms — confirming that the gain in network sensitivity does not come at the cost of focal precision.

- **Study III:** Using simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, we validate source reconstruction directly against intracranial measurements, demonstrating the ability of connectivity-informed methods to map dynamic neural networks beyond simple point-source localization.

Together, these studies establish wCSET as a principled and clinically viable tool for reconstructing distributed brain dynamics, and introduce a multi-level validation framework that moves the field beyond localization as the sole benchmark for source imaging.


# Materials and Methods

## Data Acquisition and Datasets1

### Synthetic Data

Simulations were conducted using anatomical data from a single representative subject selected from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022]. The anatomical framework consists of a T1-weighted MRI and a corresponding structural tractogram derived from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). EEG signals were simulated on a 204-channel montage derived from a 256-channel EGI HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net, after removing cheek electrodes. The cortical source space (Section 2.3.1) was parcellated into brain regions using the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022] (~400 regions, 2–10 dipoles per region). To keep the simulation budget tractable while retaining broad cortical coverage, a subset of 100 regions was selected via greedy farthest-point sampling over region centroids, yielding a spatially uniform probe set that is reused across every simulation-based analysis in this study; a separate, independently-sampled subset of 50 regions was used for the noise-robustness analysis (Section 3.1.2), where sweeping multiple SNR levels per region made the full 100-region probe set computationally prohibitive. In each simulation trial, a source region was drawn from the relevant probe set, and a spike-like waveform was assigned to all dipoles within that region, following classic simulation approaches in which epileptiform activity is modelled as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a single point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike waveform is a double Hanning window defined as:

$$
s(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$ and $W = 0.1$ s is the total spike duration — within the combined 20–200 ms range reported for interictal epileptiform discharges (spikes, 20–70 ms, and sharp waves, 70–200 ms) by consensus clinical EEG terminology [@kane_revised_2017]. The waveform consists of a dominant positive lobe spanning two-thirds of the spike duration, followed by a half-amplitude negative rebound over the remaining third, mimicking the morphology of a clinical interictal spike (Figure 1.a). The spike signal is then convolved with a Dirac comb recurring every 1 s, starting 0.5 s into a 20 s simulated recording, to generate a train of 20 spike events; these are epoched around each event and averaged into a single evoked response per simulated run, mirroring the spike-triggered averaging used to construct the clinical datasets in Studies 2 and 3.

**Propagation model.** Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner. The activity at dipole $j$ was modelled as:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $s_0(t)$ is the source waveform, $h_j$ is the number of hops (graph edges) along the shortest path from the source to dipole $j$, and $\gamma \in [0,1]$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, set to $\gamma = 0.5$: without it, activity would propagate undiminished along every reachable path and spread across the entire connectome, rather than attenuating with network distance from the source as genuine, spatially-bounded propagation should. The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along that path:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v_c} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, $v_c = 30$ mm/ms is the axonal conduction speed — at the fast end of velocities reported for large-diameter, heavily myelinated long-range cortical fibers, the kind captured by dMRI tractography [@caminiti_diameter_2013] — $\tau_p = 10$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency [@sabatini_timing_1996], and $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing. (Figure 1c).

**Noise model.** Pink noise was added at the source level to model background neural activity, and independent white noise was added at the sensor level to model measurement noise. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed target by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection. All parameters are summarised in @tbl-sim-params.

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region. The number of regions and repetitions were set via a power analysis targeting adequate sensitivity to detect a method × region interaction — i.e., whether the relative ranking of reconstruction methods depends on the anatomical location of the source, the effect of scientific interest for this study (the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design).

### Clinical Dataset A — Resection Cohort
To validate electroencephalographic source imaging clinically, we used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025, comprising 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery. Surgical outcome was assessed at 12 months post-operatively and graded on the ILAE scale (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing degrees of persistent seizures). The resected tissue serves as ground truth for localization evaluation across the full outcome range, with outcome grade retained as an explicit stratifying factor rather than pooled away: for patients with residual seizures (ILAE > 1), the resection may not have fully encompassed the true epileptogenic zone, so a source-to-resection distance is a noisier proxy for localization accuracy in that group than for seizure-free (ILAE 1) patients. Reporting results by outcome grade keeps that distinction visible rather than diluting it into a single pooled estimate. Resection masks were derived from pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI via an automated segmentation-and-registration pipeline (RAMPS; Section 2.5.1); three patients were excluded for lacking a usable mask (two failed mask generation outright, one had no post-operative T1-weighted MRI and was never processed). All remaining patients with a generated mask were retained regardless of outcome grade. Each patient's data consisted of a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording, as well as a post-operative T1-weighted MRI. The dataset provides 257-channel high-density EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net); cheek electrodes were excluded, yielding the 204-channel montage used throughout this study. Interictal epileptic discharges were visually identified and time-locked averaged at their peak.


### Clinical Dataset B — Simultaneous EEG/iEEG Cohort

To validate source reconstruction against ground-truth intracranial activity, we used a cohort of patients with simultaneously recorded scalp EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG). **FILL:** patient recruitment and diagnosis, indication for intracranial implantation (e.g. presurgical evaluation for pharmacoresistant epilepsy), electrode type (stereo-EEG vs. subdural grid/strip) and implantation rationale, number of intracranial channels, recording site, ethics approval. Interictal epileptic discharges were identified and epoched in both modalities, time-locked to the same spike events, yielding paired scalp and intracranial recordings of the same underlying activity. Each patient's data further included a pre-operative T1-weighted MRI for anatomical and forward modeling (Section 2.3), processed identically to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A); as with that cohort, individual diffusion MRI was not available for this cohort, so the structural connectome was derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (Section 2.3.3) rather than subject-specific tractography. Source reconstruction and validation results are reported for four subjects (sub-12, sub-34, sub-48, sub-50); of these, two (sub-12, sub-50) had deep sources producing no visible interictal spike on the scalp EEG, making their EEG-derived source reconstruction — and consequently the virtual iEEG projected from it (Section 2.5.2) — inherently less reliable than the remaining two. This reliability distinction is retained explicitly in the Results (Section 3.3) rather than pooled away.

## Signal Preprocessing


### EEG/iEEG Processing
<!-- Filtering, artifact rejection, and epoching (noting differences across the three datasets). -->

**Studies 1 and 3 (Simulation and Simultaneous EEG/iEEG).** EEG data were available as epochs time-locked to the interictal spike peak — the known peak of the simulated source event in Study 1, and the peak of the simultaneously recorded intracranial (iEEG) signal in Study 3, rather than a peak independently detected on the scalp EEG itself. A Common Average Reference (CAR) was applied, consistent with standard practice for source reconstruction [@bertrand_theoretical_1985]. Baseline correction was performed using the pre-spike period, and an empirical noise covariance matrix was estimated from the same baseline window for subsequent data whitening. Epochs were then averaged to obtain the evoked response: exactly 20 spike epochs per simulated run in Study 1 (Section 2.1.1), and a variable number of clinically marked interictal spikes per subject in Study 3 (130–265 across the four subjects). For the Study 3 channel-comparison analysis (Section 2.6.3), the analysis window around each spike was defined by thresholding the global field power (GFP) of the evoked response: the continuous interval around the peak over which GFP stays above a fixed number of standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline, rather than the fixed handful of samples around the peak used by @grova_intracranial_2016.

**Study 2 (Clinical Dataset A — resection cohort).** EEG data were provided as pre-averaged interictal discharge waveforms; individual epochs were not available. Preprocessing by the data providers included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines. Since individual epochs were unavailable, noise covariance estimation and data whitening were not performed. A Common Average Reference was applied. A subset of subjects presented residual 50 Hz line noise and required an additional notch filter. Baseline correction was applied to subjects whose recordings lacked it.

**iEEG (Study 3).** Intracranial recordings were available as epochs time-locked to the spike. Epochs were averaged directly to obtain the ground-truth intracranial evoked response; no further preprocessing was applied.

## Forward Modeling and Structural Priors

### Source Space

We modeled neural activity using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint. The source space was restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI data using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Approximately 7,600 dipoles (oct6 icosahedral subdivision, after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) were uniformly distributed across this surface using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013), at an average inter-dipole spacing of approximately 3.3 mm, with dipole orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source imaging because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993]. This configuration ensures that the reconstructed activity aligns with the known physiological orientation of pyramidal neurons.

### Volume Conduction Model

The forward problem involves calculating the electrical potential at the sensor locations generated by unitary dipole activity within the source space. To model the volume conduction between the sources and sensors, we employed a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989]. A standard BEM represents the interfaces between major head tissues—specifically the inner skull, outer skull, and outer skin—assuming homogeneous and isotropic electrical conductivity within each compartment. We used the MNE-Python default conductivity values of 0.3 S/m for the brain and scalp, and 0.006 S/m for the skull. This forward solution was used across all three studies.

For Study 1 only, a second forward solution was computed for source reconstruction, with the skull conductivity increased to 0.012 S/m while keeping brain and scalp conductivities unchanged at 0.3 S/m. This deliberate mismatch avoids the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004] — the circularity that arises when the same head model is used for both generating and inverting simulated data, which artificially inflates reconstruction accuracy. A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid this circularity — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014]. The two forward models differ by approximately 10% (see Figure X).

While MNE-Python typically relies on FreeSurfer’s watershed algorithm for surface extraction, this approach often yields sub-optimal geometries for BEM. To improve the accuracy of the head model, we implemented a custom pipeline: brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template. The three surfaces were fitted sequentially — inner skull first, then outer skull, then scalp — with each surface constrained to lie outside the previous one, ensuring non-intersecting layers (see Figure X). Since the EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI, they were intrinsically aligned with the resulting head model. The final forward solution (the gain matrix) was computed using MNE-Python.

### Connectivity Matrices

In this work, the brain is modeled as a graph (or connectome) where nodes represent localized brain regions - specifically dipoles in our source space - and edges represent the structural scaffolding between them. For the Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) source reconstruction method and its weighted version (wCSET), we utilize a structural connectome, where edges represent physical anatomical links.

**Empirical connectomes**

We incorporate two distinct types of structural links:
1. Long-range connections: These represent white matter tracts (axonal bundles) estimated via diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography.
2. Short-range connections: To account for local gray matter connectivity not captured by standard tractography, we connect neighboring dipoles if their geodesic distance on the cortical manifold is less than 15 mm.

To ensure physical consistency, edges are weighted by distance (in mm): fiber length for long-range tracts and geodesic distance for local connections.

**Connectome surrogates**

In clinical settings where diffusion data may be unavailable, we evaluate three connectome surrogates validated through our simulation framework (see Section 3.1). Two of these are also tested in a binarized form (edge presence only, discarding distance weights) to separate the contribution of connectome topology from that of edge-weight fidelity — the Beltrami-operator surrogate has no such counterpart, since it is not built from a weighted graph in the first place (see below) — five surrogate variants in total:

- Beltrami-operator surrogate: Eigenmodes are computed directly from the Laplace-Beltrami operator applied to the cortical mesh of each hemisphere, without ever constructing an explicit dipole-to-dipole connectome. This is the purest geometry-only control: unlike the geometry-only surrogate below, it does not threshold or weight a graph of geodesic distances at all, so there is no meaningful binarized counterpart to test (the "edges" of a continuous differential operator are not a sparse 0/1 matrix to strip weights from).
- Fused (sparse) atlas surrogate: Long-range tracts are extrapolated from the MultiConn atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], built from a reference population of 66 subjects. We parcellate the subject's brain according to the atlas and identify region pairs connected by a tract present across all 66 subjects in the reference population. Instead of connecting every dipole pair between two such atlas-connected regions, only a fraction of the possible dipole-to-dipole edges is instantiated, at a sparsity level (14%) chosen to match the edge density of a subject-level structural connectome. Gray matter connections are then added as described above.
- Geometry-only surrogate: This model relies solely on gray matter connectivity derived from the brain mesh, with nodes additionally connected across hemispheres to their homotopic (mirror-symmetric) partner to keep the resulting graph connected. While distinct from the Beltrami-operator geometry above, this surrogate tests the hypothesis that local brain geometry alone can capture significant brain-function coupling without explicit long-range information.

**Connectome perturbation**

In the simulation, one could select the connectome used to make the simulation for the source reconstruction method. But in reality, one never has the exact knowledge of the model. Therefore, we implemented a procedure to perturb the connectome before applying source reconstruction (see results 3.1.2). There are 3 types of perturbation tested individually:
- Permutation: Take an edge, delete it, and create a new one where there was none.
- Deletion: Randomly delete an edge
- Addition: Randomly add an edge

We then consider a maximum number of edits to apply, which corresponds to the number of connections in the connectome. This threshold is then set to be 100% perturbation. In the case of permutation, it means we have applied as many permutations as there are edges. For the deletion, it means every edge has been removed, leaving a fully disconnected (empty) adjacency matrix. For the addition, it means we have double the total amount of edges. While 0% corresponds to the original connectome. A connectome with no edges at all is a degenerate input for the spectral decomposition below, but not an impossible one: the graph Laplacian of a fully disconnected graph is simply the zero matrix, which still admits an (uninformative) eigendecomposition, so the reconstruction pipeline runs to completion rather than failing outright at 100% deletion — it is the meaningfulness of the resulting harmonics, not the ability to compute them, that degrades as edges are removed (Section 3.1.2).

**Graph Fourier Transform**

The connectome is mathematically represented by an adjacency matrix A, or more commonly, the graph Laplacian L, defined as L=D−A (where D is the degree matrix). This representation allows us to apply the tools of Graph Signal Processing (GSP) to neural data. The adjacency matrix actually supplied to this decomposition is the element-wise inverse of the edge distances described above, so that spatially closer, more direct structural connections (shorter fiber tracts, nearer geodesic neighbors) receive proportionally larger weight than distant ones — the natural convention for a graph meant to capture how strongly two dipoles are structurally coupled, since raw distance alone would otherwise assign the largest values to the weakest, most indirect links.

Just as the classical Fourier Transform decomposes a time-series into sine and cosine waves, the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) decomposes brain activity into a set of graph harmonics. These harmonics are the eigenvectors $u_k$ of the Graph Laplacian, obtained via the eigendecomposition: $$\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top$$
where $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the eigenvalues (graph frequencies) and $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ forms the orthonormal eigenbasis.


## Source Reconstruction Framework

For every study, we used MNE-Python's widely used methods wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA (see Section 2.4.1), and compare these to our connectivity-informed methods described in Section 2.4.2. All methods used data whitening based on an empirically estimated noise covariance matrix — a standard preprocessing step in linear M/EEG source reconstruction that decorrelates and normalizes sensor noise before inversion [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022] — with one exception: for the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), the data were provided as pre-averaged discharges with no accompanying baseline epochs, so no empirical noise covariance could be computed, and an ad-hoc (identity-like) covariance was used instead, i.e. no whitening.

### Standard Inverse Solutions

In the M/EEG inverse problem, we aim to estimate underlying dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from observed sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$. This relationship is defined by the forward model: $$\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon$$

where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix and $\epsilon$ represents additive noise. Because the number of dipoles greatly exceeds the number of sensors ($n\gg m$), the problem is ill-posed and lacks a unique solution without further constraints.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem:
$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the regularization parameter balancing data fit with prior assumptions. The matrix $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown; every method compared here replaces it with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives this family of methods its "independent-source" label throughout this work. That substitution, however, biases the resulting solution toward superficial dipoles, whose lead-field columns have systematically larger norm; the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ introduced below exists specifically to correct for this bias.

We compare wCSET and CSET against three standard, connectivity-agnostic reference methods: weighted MNE (wMNE) [@dale_improved_1993], sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], and dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000] — the three distributed source-imaging methods implemented in MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013], the toolbox used throughout this work, and thus the natural connectivity-agnostic baselines for comparison. wMNE assumes independent sources ($p=2$ in Eq. 1) with a depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ applied to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1} = \mathbf W_d, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{ii} = \frac{1}{\lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert}
$$

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to the standard literature value of 0.8 [@lin_assessing_2006]. sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting (`depth=None` in MNE-Python), since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own. CSET and wCSET, by contrast, used a depth-weighting exponent of 0.2, tuned against reconstruction accuracy in the simulation study (Section 3.1).

While it is widely accepted that source activity is heavily interdependent, these independent-source assumptions are typically chosen because estimating source co-dependence has remained computationally or theoretically elusive.

### Connectivity-Informed Inverse Solution

**Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography** (J. Rué-Queralt 2024)

Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (**CSET**) addresses the independence limitation, by operating in a **component-based space**. Instead of solving for activity in the brain's physical space, CSET projects the activity onto the **eigenmodes of the connectome** ($U$). This transforms the problem into the "connectome spectrum" space, where the prior can be more effectively described.

Given that the connectome spectrum is known to be compact, CSET enforces sparsity by applying an $l_1$​-norm to the regularizer. Let $\mathbf {\hat s}$ represent the spectrum of $\mathbf s$ (where $\mathbf s = \mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}). Equation (1) is then modified to: 
$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_1 \tag{2}
$$

The physical brain activity is then recovered via $\mathbf s^* = \mathbf U\mathbf{\hat s}^*$

**weighted CSET**

While basic CSET enforces sparsity, it does not necessarily distinguish between signal and noise in a physiologically informed way. We address this with weighted CSET (wCSET), which replaces CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior with a smooth, weighted $l_2$ prior over the connectome spectrum. Harmonic weights follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is harmonic $i$'s eigenvalue and $\beta$ controls the filter's decay rate, tuned against this connectome's own reconstruction accuracy. This form is motivated by the structure–function coupling literature: functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, i.e. a small number of low-frequency structural harmonics dominate functional coupling [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. Equation (2) thus becomes:

$$
\mathbf {\hat s}^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf U \mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h\mathbf {\hat s}\rVert_2^2 \tag{3}
$$

where $\mathbf W_h$ is the diagonal matrix of harmonic weights above. Unlike CSET's $l_1$ sparsity prior, which selects a small number of active harmonics, wCSET's $l_2$ prior smoothly downweights high-frequency harmonics while leaving the low-frequency end of the spectrum comparatively unpenalized.

Neither CSET nor wCSET is tied to a particular way of building the connectome that defines $\mathbf U$. What the framework requires is a structural graph whose edges reflect the strength of information flow between dipoles; how that graph is estimated (dMRI tractography, as used here, or an alternative such as functional-informed structural priors) and how its edges are weighted (inverse geodesic/fiber distance, as used here, but equally fiber count or raw fiber length) are choices external to the formalism itself. The specific connectome construction adopted in this work (Section 2.3.3) is one principled instantiation, motivated by the structure–function coupling literature [@abdelnour_functional_2018], not a requirement of Eq. 3.

## Clinical Ground Truth Definition

In contrast to the simulated framework, we usually do not have the exact brain activity maps to evaluate source reconstruction methods. We therefore use proxies which allow us to test specific aspects of the method. In the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2), we use the fact that patients underwent surgery, had a brain section removed, and were symptom-free of epilepsy after the surgery. We use the resected area as ground truth to measure the source localization error. We therefore need to segment the resected area (see Section 2.5.1). In the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3), we have the recordings of electric potential inside the brain, but only in a few areas. For that, we need to estimate the underlying potential generated by our reconstructed maps (which show dipole currents) at the same locations as the intracranial channels. We use for that a simplified version of the forward problem (see Section 2.5.2).

### Resected Area Segmentation

This section applies to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A; Section 2.1.2). Resection masks were generated using RAMPS, an automated segmentation-and-registration pipeline that estimates the resected volume directly from a subject's pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI. RAMPS additionally requires the hemisphere of the resection and the resected lobe (temporal, frontal, parietal, occipital, or a combination thereof) as input: the lobe was unambiguous from the clinical record for temporal resections, and was determined by visual comparison of the pre- and post-operative images for extratemporal resections. Resulting masks underwent visual quality review by overlaying the pre-operative T1w, post-operative T1w, and resection mask; subjects with a missing, incomplete, or clearly incorrect mask were excluded (Section 2.1.2).

### Source-to-iEEG Projection

This section applies to the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B; Section 2.1.3). Following source reconstruction, the estimated cortical activity was projected onto the coordinates of the intracranial electrodes to generate "virtual" iEEG potentials. This projection followed the methodology of **Grova et al. (2016)**. Given that this step assumes the sources and sensors reside within the same compartment, we modeled this as an infinite homogeneous conduction problem. The potential $\Phi$ at a location $r$ is estimated from the brain activity as:
$$
\Phi(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3}
$$

Following the adjustments proposed by **Cosandier-Rimélé
et al. 2007**, the brain tissue conductivity (σ) was set to **0.25 S/m**(modified from the standard **0.33 S/m**) to compensate for the simplifications inherent in the homogeneous model. Assuming an iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy of 3 mm, we use the same model adjustement to prevent instabilities of the model caused by too close measurements: $$\begin{align}\Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r>r_0 = 3 \text{ mm} \\ \Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r\ler_0 = 3 \text{ mm}\end{align}$$

## Performance Evaluation Metrics

### Map to map comparison

To evaluate each method we compute the (signed) Pearson spatial correlation between the reconstructed and ground-truth activity maps at each time point:
$$
\mathcal{C}(t) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{true}}(i) \cdot \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{est}}(i)}{\sigma_{\text{true}}(t) \cdot \sigma_{\text{est}}(t)}
$$

where $\mathbf s^t_{x}(i)$ is the activity at dipole $i$ and time $t$, and $\sigma_{x}(t)$ is the standard deviation of map $x$ at time $t$.

### Localization Accuracy

To evaluate localization accuracy, the source onset of the interictal spikes was defined at 50% of the rising phase, following the methodology of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020: this time point is a pragmatic compromise between a low probability that the source has already started propagating (favoring the discharge's onset) and an adequate signal-to-noise ratio (favoring the discharge's peak, by which point the source has typically already spread). The Euclidean distance was then calculated between the estimated source location and the target mask — the true seed region for the simulation dataset, or the resection volume for the resection cohort. Rather than working around voxel-grid discretization by averaging distances to several nearest voxels, we follow @carboni_linear_2022 and @wang_geometry_2026 and report the minimum Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the mask boundary, taken as 0 mm whenever that location already lies inside the mask.


### Channel comparison

To evaluate the accuracy of the spatial reconstruction, the projected virtual iEEG activity (Section 2.5.2) was compared against the recorded ground-truth iEEG using a battery of complementary similarity metrics, each computed in three modes: spatial (across channels, per time point), temporal (across time, per channel), and spatio-temporal (a single scalar over the full window). All metrics are polarity-invariant, since an overall sign flip is an arbitrary consequence of the virtual-electrode reference convention rather than a meaningful failure mode:

- Pearson correlation and cosine similarity between estimated and ground-truth channel activity, in each of the three modes above, made polarity-invariant by taking the absolute value of the raw statistic ($|r|$, $|\cos|$) rather than the signed value — a plain correlation or cosine similarity is not itself polarity-invariant, so this absolute-value step is what removes the sign-flip ambiguity.
<!-- Explained variance of the ground-truth activity by the estimated activity is still computed and saved for every subject/method (polarity-invariant by taking the better of the score on the signal and on its negation, since R² isn't sign-symmetric the way correlation/cosine are), but not yet featured in the main results below -- kept here as a note pending further investigation, mirroring how processing_simf.qmd still computes but doesn't plot precision/AP (see plot_configuration.py above). -->
- Correlation between estimated and ground-truth relative energy maps (REM), computed spatially and temporally; polarity-invariant by construction, since it is built from squared energy rather than raw amplitude.

For each competing method, we additionally compute a win-rate against wCSET — the fraction of channels (or time points) on which wCSET's estimate is closer to ground truth than the competitor's — summarizing pairwise performance across this metric set relative to our proposed method, rather than a full all-against-all comparison across every method pair.

To test the impact of neglecting source dependences we created a simulation that is constrained by the structural connectivity. This allows us to have simulated EEG recordings with complex ground truth activity. Figure 3.1.a shows an example of an EEG recording with the key events happening. We have the peak phase, where the EEG signal is highest. At that phase, similar to what is suggested in the literature, the source has already started to propagate. Generally, it is advised to reconstruct around 50% of the rising phase (or even before if the signal to noise permits it) to properly locate the source [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]. We consider as the source propagation phase everything happening after 50% rising phase until the signal is back to noise level. We then applied source reconstruction using the five methods described in Section 2.4 (wMNE, sLORETA, dSPM, and the connectivity-informed CSET and wCSET). We did source localization to compare the accuracy of source localization. At single-trial SNR = 10, wCSET achieved significantly lower localization error than sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region, FDR-corrected: sLORETA p < 0\.0001, effect size r = \-0\.48; dSPM p < 0\.0001, r = \-0\.54; wMNE p < 0\.0001, r = \-1\.00, i.e. wCSET's error was lower in every single paired region), while the difference against CSET did not reach significance (p = 0\.081, r = \-0\.20). Median localization error was 3\.9 mm for wCSET, 6\.8 mm for CSET, 10\.2 mm for sLORETA, and 12\.7 mm for dSPM — all comparable in absolute terms, well within the size of a typical resection volume — whereas wMNE was a clear outlier at 59\.0 mm, consistent with its lack of noise normalization. Effect sizes therefore support a picture in which the four noise-normalized or connectivity-informed methods localize the source similarly well at this phase, with wMNE as the sole exception.

We also computed the spatial correlation time point by time point between the simulated ground truth and the reconstructions for all our source reconstruction methods. This allows us to estimate which method is best for reconstructing the source propagation. For statistical validation, we repeated the simulation 8 times for each of 100 spatially-uniform sample regions (Section 2.1.1). We then computed the median spatial correlation, together with its interquartile range across simulated runs, and plotted it over time in Figure 3. Localization error increased for every method as SNR decreased, but the onset and severity of this degradation differed sharply across methods (Figure below, left). wMNE was affected soonest and most severely: already comparable to dSPM at the highest SNR tested (median 14\.4 mm at SNR=20), its error rose to 61–74 mm by SNR≤10 — significantly worse than wCSET across the entire SNR range (region-paired cluster-permutation, p_corrected = 0\.001, Cohen's dz = 3\.18). sLORETA followed a similar but less extreme pattern, remaining in the 9–16 mm range down to SNR=5 before climbing to 36–59 mm at SNR≤2, and was likewise significantly worse than wCSET across the whole range (p_corrected = 0\.001, dz = 0\.99). In the simulation, the true connectome is known; in practice it never is exactly. To test what happens when the wrong connectome is used, we systematically perturbed the true connectome before reconstruction (Section 2.3.3) and re-evaluated localization error and spatial correlation for CSET and wCSET. dSPM and sLORETA are connectome-agnostic and are not recomputed per degradation level; they appear only as flat reference lines in the figures below.

wCSET's localization error remained essentially flat under permutation up to 60% (4\.0–6\.5 mm), only climbing noticeably beyond that point (9\.3 mm at 70%, 16\.7 mm at 100%); under deletion it was even more stable, staying within 3\.9–4\.5 mm through 80% before collapsing at 90% (13\.6 mm) and catastrophically at 100% (57\.8 mm, consistent with Section 2.3.3's note that a fully disconnected connectome yields a degenerate spectral basis). Under addition, both methods were essentially insensitive to the perturbation across the full range tested. CSET was significantly worse than wCSET for both permutation (region-paired cluster-permutation: 0–20%, p_corrected = 0\.003, Cohen's dz = 0\.51; 50–100%, p_corrected = 0\.001, dz = 0\.73) and deletion (0–80%, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 0\.80) — but this reversed sharply at 90–100% deletion, where CSET became significantly *more* accurate than wCSET (p_corrected = 0\.001, dz = \-1\.52; median 14\.2 mm for CSET vs. 57\.8 mm for wCSET at 100%), indicating that CSET's sparser L1 harmonic selection is more robust than wCSET's smooth weighting once the connectome is almost entirely destroyed. Under addition, the two methods differed significantly only at the very first step (0–10%, p_corrected = 0\.020, dz = 0\.46), and were statistically indistinguishable from 20% onward.

Spatial correlation with the ground truth showed the pattern anticipated: permutation slowly degraded wCSET's correlation (0\.75 at 0% down to 0\.14 at 100%), while CSET's own correlation stayed comparatively flat through 60% (0\.40–0\.50) before also declining sharply thereafter (0\.09 at 100%) — but wCSET remained significantly higher than CSET across the entire permutation range (region-paired cluster-permutation, p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 2\.55), confirming that CSET's greater apparent stability up to 60% is stability at a lower level, not a genuine advantage. Both methods were far more robust to deletion and addition: wCSET's correlation stayed within 0\.70–0\.75 through 80% deletion (collapsing to 0\.59 at 90% and 0\.22 at 100%, mirroring the localization-error collapse above) and within 0\.67–0\.75 across the entire addition range; CSET again stayed nearly flat throughout both (0\.42–0\.48 for deletion through 90%, 0\.46–0\.52 for addition). wCSET was significantly better than CSET across the entire tested range for both deletion (p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 2\.04) and addition (p_corrected < 0\.001, dz = 1\.74).

In clinical settings, subject-specific dMRI is often unavailable. We therefore tested whether cruder, dMRI-free connectome surrogates (Section 2.3.3) could replace the true connectome without materially harming CSET/wCSET's accuracy, comparing each surrogate directly against the original connectome for each method.

For localization error, wCSET's accuracy was statistically indistinguishable from using the true connectome for every surrogate tested (paired Wilcoxon vs. original connectome, region-paired: beltrami p = 0\.488; fused p = 0\.282; fused-bin p = 0\.247; geom-atlas p = 0\.279; geom-atlas-bin p = 0\.247 — none significant). CSET was more sensitive to the choice of surrogate: it was significantly worse than the original connectome with the beltrami (p_corrected < 0\.001, effect size r = \-0\.48) and fused (p_corrected = 0\.025, r = \-0\.19) surrogates, but statistically indistinguishable from original with the binarized fused (p = 0\.267), geom-atlas (p = 0\.315), and geom-atlas-bin (p = 0\.315) surrogates. Localization is thus similar across every surrogate for wCSET specifically, essentially insensitive to which surrogate replaces the true connectome.

For spatial correlation, differences from the original connectome were statistically significant for nearly every surrogate and method, but effect sizes were often small, and not all significant differences pointed the same direction. The beltrami surrogate produced the largest, most consistent drop in correlation relative to the original connectome, for both CSET (p_corrected < 0\.001 at both phases, r = 0\.64–0\.68) and wCSET (p_corrected < 0\.001 at both phases, r = 0\.58–0\.90) — yet even this worst case remained far more accurate than the connectome-agnostic references: wCSET's correlation with beltrami (median 0\.54 half rising phase, 0\.55 peak) was still roughly 3–4× higher than dSPM's (0\.14, 0\.15) or sLORETA's (0\.15, 0\.17) flagship performance with the true connectome. CSET was significantly worse than original with every other surrogate too, though with shrinking effect sizes — from fused (r = 0\.70 half rising phase, 0\.76 peak) and fused-bin (r = 0\.48, 0\.42) down to geom-atlas and geom-atlas-bin, where the peak-phase effect was small (r = 0\.14–0\.18, though still p_corrected < 0\.05). wCSET's pattern was more favorable still: the fused and fused-bin surrogates were associated with significantly *higher* correlation than the original connectome (fused: p_corrected < 0\.001 half rising phase, p_corrected = 0\.001 peak; fused-bin: p_corrected < 0\.001 half rising phase, p_corrected < 0\.001 peak), and geom-atlas/geom-atlas-bin were significantly higher at half rising phase (p_corrected < 0\.001) but statistically indistinguishable from original at peak (p = 0\.930, p = 0\.951). Together with the localization results, this indicates wCSET's accuracy is not merely insensitive to the connectome surrogate used, but for spatial correlation specifically, several cruder dMRI-free surrogates perform as well as, or nominally better than, the subject's own tractography-derived connectome.

## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG)

### Spatial and Temporal Correlation Analysis

Source localization was inconclusive for connectivity-informed methods in Study II — comparable to, but not clearly better than, standard methods (Section 3.2.1). Because these methods are designed to capture distributed activity rather than a single focal source, we instead tested whether they better reproduce the overall pattern of activity, as the simulation results in Section 3.1 suggest they should.

Of the four subjects with usable simultaneous EEG/iEEG data (Section 2.1.3), two (sub-34, sub-48) show a visible interictal spike on the scalp EEG, while the remaining two (sub-12, sub-50) have deep sources producing no visible spike on the EEG despite clear intracranial evidence of the same interictal discharge. For each subject we compared wCSET against every competitor at the level of individual channels (temporal correlation: how well each channel's own time-course matches the true intracranial recording) and individual timepoints (spatial correlation: how well the pattern across channels matches at each instant), using a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (n_eff) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count, since neighbouring channels and timepoints from the same subject and spike are not independent observations.

For the two subjects without a visible scalp EEG spike, sub-12 showed no significant difference from any competitor in either mode (smallest p_corrected = 0\.096, vs. CSET temporally), consistent with an EEG-derived reconstruction too unreliable at the source to distinguish methods at all. Sub-50 was the exception, and its result cuts the other way: temporally, wCSET remained significantly better than CSET (p_corrected = 0\.003, n_eff=86), but spatially the pattern reversed — sLORETA, dSPM, and CSET all significantly outperformed wCSET (p_corrected = 0\.003–0\.015; wMNE trended the same direction but did not reach significance, p_corrected = 0\.063). This is the one case in the cohort where standard, connectivity-agnostic methods matched the true intracranial activity pattern better than wCSET, at least spatially.
